title: Quick Heal Flags the Four Diwali Shopping Scams Most Likely to Reach Your Phone
excerpt: Lookalike stores, fake support numbers, OTP-hunting 'delivery executives' and QR-code refunds are this season's traps — plus the checks that stop each one.
body:
• Quick Heal has warned Diwali shoppers about four recurring scam setups: lookalike stores reached from social-media ads, fake customer-support numbers, delivery executives fishing for OTPs, and QR-code 'refunds'.
  • The core UPI rule: a PIN authorises money leaving your account — it is never required to receive a payment or a refund.
  • Reach businesses only through bookmarked websites, verified apps or numbers on official pages, and check the recipient name and amount before approving any payment.
  • If you are scammed in India, call the cybercrime helpline 1930 and report at cybercrime.gov.in immediately, then alert your bank.

Festival shopping concentrates everything scammers need — hurried buyers, heavy discounts and a flood of delivery messages. Cybersecurity firm Quick Heal has laid out the specific setups it expects to circulate this Diwali, in an advisory reported by SMEStreet.

The four moments that need attention

Quick Heal's scenarios share one mechanism: shifting your trust from a recognised brand to a channel the scammer controls. A consumer sees a social-media advertisement and lands on a lookalike store. A shopper searching for customer support calls a fraudulent number displayed online. A supposed delivery executive asks for an OTP to "confirm" an address. A seller claims a payment failed and sends a QR code for a refund — scanning it, and entering a PIN, sends money out instead.

"Technology can detect many warning signs, but an informed user who refuses to be rushed adds a crucial layer of protection."

— Harish Kumar G S, CEO, Quick Heal Technologies

The habits that break the script

The company's countermeasures are deliberately mundane. Reach businesses through bookmarked websites, verified applications or contact details published on official pages — not through links in messages. Read URLs carefully, especially where letters have been replaced, added or rearranged. Download apps only from official app stores and refuse files sent through messages. Before approving a UPI payment, check the recipient's name and amount — and remember that a UPI PIN authorises money leaving an account; it is never required to receive money.

Quick Heal also advises keeping operating systems, browsers and apps updated, enabling multi-factor authentication wherever available, using unique passwords for shopping, email and financial accounts, watching transaction alerts so unauthorised activity surfaces quickly, and enabling payment limits to reduce exposure. Its own festive-season guide makes the same point about urgency: "only today," "limited cashback" and "claim your reward now" are pressure devices, and the correct response to any of them is to open the retailer's official app yourself and check whether the offer exists.

For families shopping across borders

The same scripts target diaspora shoppers ordering gifts for delivery in India and relatives paying on their behalf. The ten-minute version of this article — show an older parent one fake delivery message and walk through the OTP rule before the festival rush — does more than any single app. If a scam succeeds, speed is the only lever left: in India, report on the 1930 helpline and cybercrime.gov.in at once, and call the bank to freeze what can still be frozen.

steps.step: Reach stores through bookmarks or official apps
steps.detail: Never shop through links in WhatsApp, SMS or social-media ads — type the address yourself and read the URL for swapped or added letters.

steps.step: Never share an OTP or scan a refund QR code
steps.detail: A UPI PIN only authorises money leaving your account; receiving a refund never requires it. Delivery staff never need your OTP to confirm an address.

steps.step: Check the recipient name and amount before approving any UPI payment
steps.detail: Scammers rename accounts to look like brands. Verify before you approve, and enable payment limits to cap exposure.

steps.step: Turn on multi-factor authentication and unique passwords
steps.detail: Use different passwords for shopping, email and banking, keep apps and browsers updated, and watch transaction alerts for unauthorised activity.

steps.step: If money is gone, report immediately
steps.detail: In India, call the national cybercrime helpline 1930 and file a report at cybercrime.gov.in, then contact your bank to block the card or flag the transaction.
